subject: Cognitive Science
title: Fear and Decision Making
description: A quick win: understand Fear and Decision Making.

hook.text: After the 9/11 attacks, 1,500 extra Americans died in car accidents—they avoided flying out of fear.

buildup.text: Fear distorts risk assessment. It makes rare dangers feel imminent and safe choices feel reckless.

discovery.text: The amygdala hijacks decision-making during fear, bypassing slower, rational evaluation systems.

twist.text: This was adaptive for predators on the savanna. For modern risks involving statistics, it backfires.

climax.text: Fear doesn't just color one decision—it shifts your entire risk threshold, making you cautious about everything.

quiz.question: What happened to U.S. car deaths after 9/11?
options: They increased as people avoided flying

details.summary: Fear narrows attention, increases risk aversion, and biases choices toward safety even when the threat is minimal. It can also spill over: fear from one source makes unrelated risks seem more dangerous.
details.whyItMatters: Fear distorts risk assessment. Policies made in fear, from overspending on security to avoiding beneficial risks, carry enormous social and economic costs.
takeaways: Fear increases risk aversion beyond rational levels
Incidental fear spills over to unrelated judgments

faq.question: How does fear spill over to unrelated decisions?
faq.answer: Watching a scary movie makes people rate unrelated risks as higher. Fear activates a general threat state that colors all subsequent judgments. The emotion itself becomes a source of information, people infer that because they feel afraid, the situation must be dangerous.

faq.question: Is all fear-based decision-making bad?
faq.answer: No. Fear is adaptive when it matches actual threat level. Fear of speeding keeps you safe. The problem arises when fear is disproportionate or misapplied to low-risk situations. Calibrating fear responses to actual risk, rather than vividness or media exposure, is the key challenge.
